div.head: Again the book of the Kohelet; and there are in it six sections.

div.ab:
Firstly, proem. Solomon wrote this book in his old age, and because it contains amazing wisdom concerning the vanity of this material world, he assembled the whole nation and recited it before them. And because of this he called himself in it (the book) Koheleth, that is to say, the gatherer. And its objects are three: firstly, he teaches, indeed, about the transitoriness of this world; secondly, he
rebukes the wealthy; and thirdly, he adminishes the poor that they shall not complain.

div.head: Section One.
div.ab:
Section One. (1:2) Vanities of vanities; i. e., emptiness of emptinesses. The Hebrew designates by a thing which does not abide, and some say that in Syriac means vapour, but they did not judge with accuracy, for with a Pethoho of He and Zeqofo of Beth stopped, means vapour, but not with a Revoso of He and vowellessness of Beth fricative. And five times does he repeat this word, a type of the five bodily senses, the pleasure of which does not endure nor does their annoyance last. (1:3) What profit has man in all the labor which he labors under the sun; i. e., in this world, from accumulation of wealth by labor. (1:4) A generation passes and a generation comes, i. e., times change, but the earth abides forever; i. e., as long as this world stands, that is to say, until the time of its renewal, for we have shown in our dialectical or philosophical books
that the elements will not become nothingness at the end but they will only be renewed. (1:5) The sun arises and the sun goes down, i. e., here he shows that the movement that causes the day is from East to the West. (1:6) He goes towards the South and turns around towards the North, i. e., and here he makes known that the movement that causes the four yearly seasons is from West to East, combined with the northward and southward declinations. To its circuits (with a Zeqofo of heth) returns, i. e., turns back, the wind; i. e., to the lodgings of the sun. (1:7) All the rivers empty into the sea; yet the sea does not become full; i. e., the rivers are the animals that procreate and the sea is the world. (1:8) And all things are weary; i. e., because of the nature of this world. (1:9) That which was is, and there is no thing new under the sun; i. e., the species of things are already created and there will not be a new creation again but the individuals of the essences come into being and cease to be. (1:13) Sore travail has God given unto men that they shall be busy by it, i. e., because they did not keep the commandment, He ordained (that) their sustenance (should be obtained) by toil. (1:14) And behold everything is vanity; i. e., transitory. (1:15) That which is crooked cannot be made straight; i. e., without divine assistance, and that which is wanting cannot be counted; i. e., as (being) perfect.
(1:18b) He who (desires) to know more, increases sorrow; i. e., without vigilance and labors wisdom cannot be acquired. (1:18) For, in much wisdom is much grief; i. e., he who knows more grieves more for the people that go astray from the truth, and for his soul which is submerged in this world as in a sea.

(2:8) I got me man praisers and woman praisers; i. e., men singers and women singers, man cupbearers and female cupbearers; i. e., youths and maidens to serve wine. (2:9) also my wisdom stopped, i. e., it was amazed when it noticed that all the desires pass away. (2:12) For who is the man that may enter after the king in judgment, i. e., if to a worldly king man cannot say why have you done so, how can he say (this) to God who created him. (2:14) The same event happens to all of them; i. e., death. (2:24) There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink; i. e., with a measure, and show himself pleasure in his labor, i. e., God created him for this.

div.head: Section Two.
div.ab: Section Two. (3:2) There is a time to beget and a time to die, i. e., he does not counsel us to do these things, but he demonstrates that the courses of this world are impermanent and changeable. (3:11) And the world did he set in their hearts, i. e., the love of the world. (3:14) The Lord has made that (men) should fear Him, i. e., He gave them strength to worship Him. (3:16) In the place of justice there is wickedness, i. e., because men are judging, but at the end when God will judge, it will not be so. (3:19) And there is no preeminence of man above the beast, i. e., they die alike. (3:21) Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of beast goes down into the earth, i. e., few are those who know the incorruptibility of the rational soul.

(4:1) Might (with Zeqofo of Yodh) and there is no helper; i. e., there is he who looks for help and no one will sustain him. (Lit.: no man holds him by his hand.) (4:5) The fool folds his hands and eats his flesh; i. e., he kisses his hands that give him his desires. (4:14) For out of a house of prisoners he came forth to reign; i. e., from the house of poverty. (4:15) With the second youth that will stand up in his stead; i. e., after an old fool, a young man who is poor but wise, will reign. (4:16) And also others will not rejoice in him; i. e., soon he gets a proud spirit and he oppresses those who made him king, for his childishness destroys his wisdom.

div.head: Section Three.
div.ab: Section Three. (4:17) Guard thy foot when thou goest to the house of God; i. e., your thoughts shall not be distracted.

(5:1) Let not thy heart be hasty to utter a word before God; i. e., vow nothing but that which you will be able to fulfill. (5:7) For he who is high above the high keeps watch; i. e., God will take vengeance from the wrong doers. (5:8) The King cultivates the field; i. e., when he sees a cultivated field he wishes to seize it. (5:19) Because not for a long time will he remember the days of his life (with Revoso of nun), i. e., he does not experience the greater part of his pleasures in his days. For God makes him busy (with Pethoho of Nun) with pleasure; i. e., only those who are oppressed count their days.

(6:9) Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the soul; i. e., actions are better than illusion. (6:10) That which has been was called by its name long ago; i. e., that which God previously knew that it would happen, happened.

(7:1) A good name is better than precious oil; i. e., good deeds that are the cause of a good name are better for man than all the possessions that he acquired and left for others. And the day of death is better than the day of
birth; i. e., for if man does not die he cannot live eternally. (7:3) Anger is better than laughter; i. e., because laughter is wantonness of the heart and anger the strength of the soul.

div.head: Section Four.
div.ab: Section Four. (7:4) The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; i. e., because they know the end of things. But the heart of the fools is in the house of mirth; i. e., because they care only for that which is prepared. (7:8) Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof; i. e., because silence is better than speech. (7:12) For the shadow of wisdom is like the shadow of money; i. e., it pleases its possessor. (7:13) To make straight (with Pethoho of Nun) that which He made crooked. (7:14) And consider the day of adversity, i. e., be careful, concerning the saying that man cannot find after him, i. e., that man cannot say there happened to me what has not happened to others. (7:15) I have seen a righteous man who perished in his righteousness; i. e., who became despised. (7:16) Be not righteous overmuch; i. e., do not consider in your own eyes that you are more righteous than all men. And do not make thyself overwise, so that you may not be stupified; i. e., do not make thyself overwise so that you might not be asked for great things and fail.

(8:1) Who knows the wise man and who knows the interpretation of the thing; i. e., of that (passage) that God has made man upright and they have sought many empty ideas. (8:8) There is no man who has power over the wind to retain the wind, i. e., man has no power to keep away corruption from his
nature. (8:10) And so I saw the wicked buried, and they are coming, i. e., they who buried them return and remember them with kindness, forgetting their evil deeds.

div.head: Section Five.
div.ab: Section Five. (8:14) For there are righteous men unto whom there comes (recompense) according to the work of the wicked; and the reverse, i. e., he expresses himself wonderingly, and he continues to say about it. (8:16) I applied my heart to know wisdom, i. e., I might understand the cause of these.

(9:3) Madness (with a Pethoho of Pe and Zeqofo of He). (9:8) Let thy garments be always white, i. e., let thy actions be correct.
(10:1) Great foolishness is more honored than wisdom and great glory, i. e., by the fools great foolishness is more honored than wisdom. (10:2) The heart of a wise man is at his right hand, the heart of a fool is at his left; i. e., the one is fed by right (thoughts), the other by the reverse. (10:4) For the healing art forgives sins; i. e., when the ruler will oppress you, endure, and your sins will be forgiven.

div.head: Section Six.
div.ab: Section Six. (10:8) He who breaks down (the Greek reads, he who pulls out) a fence, a serpent shall bite him (with stopping of Qof and fricativeness of Tau), i. e., he who transgresses the law will perish. (10:9) He who removes stones shall be hurt by them (with Pethoho of Qof and alif), i. e., he who changes the borders. (10:16) Woe to thee, O Land, whose king is a child, i. e., whose reason is deficient. And thy princes feast in the morning; i. e., they care for their own advantage rather than the advantage of the people.

(11:1) Cast thy bread upon the waters; i. e., be liberal. (11:2) Give a portion to seven also to eight; i. e., bequeath for both worlds, for eight is the symbol of the new world. (11:4) He that observes the wind shall not
sow and he that regards the clouds shall not reap; i. e., give your alms in and out of season.

(12:2) Before the sun becomes dark and the light of the moon and the stars; i. e., before your senses fail. And the clouds return after the rain; i. e., and you will enter Sheol after you will weep. (12:3) In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, i. e., the bones. And men of might shall be agitated; i. e., the tendons and veins that bear mental, vital and physical force. And the grinders cease; i. e., the teeth. And those that look out through the windows shall become dark; i. e., the eyes. (12:4) And the doors shall be shut in the streets, i. e., the mouth and the outlet. And one shall arise at the voice of a bird,
i. e., when the terror of death will seize him, and like a bird, his word will not be understood; i. e., when he will stammer. And all the daughters of praise shall be brought low; i. e., the beauty of the limbs. (12:5) And he will also be afraid of the high; i. e., of evil spirits which lurk in the air. And the wakefulness will spring up suddenly upon him (with Revoso of Nun), i. e., thoughts will arise in him which will disturb his sleep. And the almond tree shall flourish (with a Zeqofo of sin and Qussaya of Dalath); death will come soon just as the bitter almond blossoms before all the trees, And the locust will multiply, i. e., pains. And the henna plant will be scattered, i. e., the body will become relaxed and will exhale its foulness. And the Baishonic herbs will fade, i. e., the proud things, which are like the mountains of Bashan, will vanish. (And in the Greek) the lily will fade, i. e., beauty. (12:6) Before the silver cord will be severed, i. e., trade, by means of which people are bound together as with a cord, and the rose apple will be shattered; i. e., the testicles, genital organs. And the pitcher will break at the fountain, i. e., at the mouth of the Sheol which swallows up, and will bring forth again at the resurrection. And the wheel will hasten to the pit; i. e., the body to the grave. (12:11) Masters of thresholds were given from one shepherd; i. e., the teachings were given from God to men. (12:13) The end of the matter in its summing up; i. e., take care that your end shall be good in word as well as in act. (12:14) And God shall bring all matters in judgment; i. e.,
he shows that he believes in resurrection and judgment, and the multitude of the preceding words (against resurrection and judgment) he quoted as from the mouth of others.
The Book of Koheleth is finished with its comments.

noteGrp.note: p. 26, n. 1 The same is found in the Yalkut. It reads as follows: Rabbi Jonathan said, Solomon wrote Song of Songs first, then Proverbs, and after that, Ecclesiastes. Rabbi Jonathan then compares it to the life of man who in youth composes songs, who as he becomes more mature speaks of parables, and who in his old age expresses words of pessimism.

p. 26, n. 2 The Yalkut Shimoni says on this verse, The text reads, The words of Koheleth and not, The words of Solomon because his words were spoken in an assembly. Rabbi Huna in the name of Rabbi Acha said, One group entered and one group left to hear his wisdom. Rabbi Isaac said, Because of the verse, Then Solomon assembled (I Kings, 8:1) he was called Koheleth, son of David.

p. 27, n. 1 The Madrash Raba remarks on this verse, In all his labors. Shall we assume that it refers to the toil of the Torah? Therefore it is written, In all his labors. He should not toil for his own labors, but he should toil for the Torah. Ibid. He explains this verse in a similar way, That he labors under the sun of the work which he labors under the sun he has no benefit, but of the labor which is above the sun he has a benefit.
p. 28, n. 1 Lit.: by the help of.

p. 29, n. 1 Here again the Midrash Raba makes a somewhat similar remark which is as follows: If any person will say to you I can understand the substance of the world, then say to him, If you cannot understand the work of a mortal king, how then can you understand the work of God, who is King of Kings.
p. 30, n. 1 This text is not found in this form in any editions of the Peshitta, nor in the Massoretic text.
p. 30, n. 1 This text is not found in this form in any editions of the Peshitta, nor in the Massoretic text.
p. 31, n. 1 The Madrash Raba explains this verse in the following manner: Good oil is beneficial only in its time, but a good name lasts forever.
p. 33, n. 1 This similar idea is expressed here in the Midrash Raba: Man has no power over his own spirit to keep it away from him.

p. 33, n. 2 The same thought is expressed in Midrash Rabba on this verse. It reads as follows: Rabbi Jochanan Ben Zakkai said, The verse cannot have relation to the white garments and fat oils, for the heathens also have many white garments and fat oils. It can only refer to the (Biblical) laws and good actions and (studying) Torah.
p. 34, n. 1 Targum - And a people who transgresses the law of God and breaks the fence of the world will fall into the hand of a wicked king, who will bite them like a serpent.
p. 35, n. 1 Babli Tractate Sabbath, pp. 152a, gives a similar interpretation: These are the loins and the ribs.
p. 35, n. 2 Ibid. And the grinders cease; these are the teeth:
p. 35, n. 3 Babli Tractate Sabbath, pp. 152a, gives the same interpretation to this verse: Those are the eyes.
p. 35, n. 4 Ibid. And the doors shall be shut in the street, i. e., these are the openings to the human body.
